name: Lash Lure

card.summary: Lash Lure was a 1930s coal-tar eyelash and eyebrow dye sold to darken lashes, whose eye injuries helped drive the 1938 US cosmetics law.
card.note: Contained para-phenylenediamine; withdrawn after documented eye injuries.

quick.overview:
Lash Lure was an eyelash and eyebrow dye made by the Cosmetic Manufacturing Company of Los Angeles in the early 1930s. It promised lastingly dark lashes and brows, and its active ingredient was para-phenylenediamine (PPD), a coal-tar dye.

Some women suffered severe reactions to it, including corneal damage and, in one confirmed case, permanent blindness. The FDA showed it in its 1933 "Chamber of Horrors" exhibit, and it was reportedly the first product seized after the 1938 Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
quick.how: It was applied to lashes and brows as a dye intended to be semi-permanent. It is a historical product no longer sold.
quick.risks: Injuries reported included swelling, lash and brow loss and eye damage. One woman became blind after an allergic reaction and an infection that followed brow plucking before dyeing. The FDA treated PPD in eyelash dyes as an adulterant.

lead: Lash Lure was a coal-tar-based eyelash and eyebrow dye of the early 1930s, made by the Cosmetic Manufacturing Company of Los Angeles. It was used to give longer-lasting dark lashes and brows [1].

Its active ingredient was para-phenylenediamine (PPD) [1]. Several women suffered corneal damage, and one became totally blind after an allergic reaction and an infection reported to follow brow plucking before dyeing [1].

The FDA included it in its traveling exhibit, which a reporter called the American Chamber of Horrors because all the products were legal under the 1906 law [2]. Coverage was cited as contributing to the 1938 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, which brought cosmetics under regulation [2][3].

chain: Dye applied to lashes and brows
Historic injuries led to cosmetics regulation
angle.text: It darkened lashes and brows as a lasting dye. Its history is documented mainly for the harm it caused and the law that followed.

paras: A Paramount newsreel in October 1933 referred to an unnamed eyelash beautifier, and mascara sales reportedly dropped. The FDA displayed the case at the Chicago World's Fair in 1933, and TIME covered it in December 1933 [1].

The 1938 Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, signed 25 June 1938, brought cosmetics under regulation and prohibits marketing adulterated cosmetics [2][3]. Lash Lure was reportedly the first product seized under it, and the FDA told dye makers that PPD in lash and brow dyes was an adulteration, effectively ending its US use [1].
The FDA describes the product as injuring many women's eyes, including one confirmed case of permanent blindness [2]. PPD is now considered a potent allergen [1].

timeline.event: Shown in the FDA's Chamber of Horrors exhibit; newsreel covers injuries [1][2].
Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act signed 25 June; Lash Lure seized [1][3].
